transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The GOP is confronting a midterm reckoning in Florida, where Republicans fended off
Democratic rivals, including for governor.
Outgoing governor, Ron DeSantis, said what happened last night in many parts of the United
States was close to a, quote, "extinction-level event for Republicans."
At the White House today, President Trump said he'd probably get along with the Democrats
when they take control of Congress in January, but he says he still has the power to veto.
He agreed with Vice President J.D. Vance's assessment today that voters who broke with
the GOP did so over the war with Iran.
Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term,
and probably that's, probably it's true.
President Trump says he'd go to war again if he had to because of Iran's nuclear threat.
NPR's Tamara Keith takes a closer look at a political map that appeared to buck the
GOP's attempts at gaining the edge through redistricting.
All of the races that leaned Democratic heading in are either called for Democrats or headed
in that direction.
All of the toss-up seats have been called for Democrats or headed in that direction.
And then in the lean Republican seats, it's a bit more of a mixed story.
We're waiting on a lot of results in that column, but Democrats are ahead in a number
of those too.
NPR's Barbara Sprout reports the Senate's top Democrats says the party's victories in
the midterms represent a "generational remake" of the Senate map.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer says the voters entrusted Democrats to ease their
economic burdens.
We are going to work hard to drive costs down with the president or without him.
While President Trump hasn't shied away from saying he'll use his veto pen on Democratic
legislative priorities, he's also signaled some openness to cutting deals with the next
Democratic-controlled Congress.
Schumer also said Democrats will root out what he called corruption in the Trump administration.
Barbara Sprout, NPR News, Washington.
One of the biggest upsets was in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews flipped a Republican-held
Senate seat in defeating Darlene Graham.
NPR's Selena Simmons-Definses Andrews will be the Senate's first Democratic practicing
physician since the 1930s.
Many new physician lawmakers, including Andrews, were recruited and backed by a group called
314 Action, which invested $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates running for
state or federal office.
Many of them won, including public health officials Abdul El Sayed for the Michigan
Senate seat and Amy Acton for Ohio governor.
Shaughnessy Naughton tells NPR that the candidates benefited from health care being a top issue
during the campaign.
The insecurity that people are feeling over the price of everything and just so much becoming
out of reach.
Polls show the American public trusts doctors much more than other experts, which may have
helped to boost these candidates.
Selena Simmons-Definses, reporting, it's NPR News.
The Dow has surged today, closing up more than 1,500 points for more than 3 percent.
NPR's Rafael Nam explains the rally.
There were two main reasons.
First, we did not get a contested election, which many investors had feared would lead
to volatility.
Instead, President Trump said he would accept the results.
Secondly, investors also tend to prefer divided government because they think it can prevent
potential excesses.
But it's not clear if the stock market gains will be sustained.
Democrats could pursue stronger regulations against businesses, especially when it comes
to AI and data centers.
And Elon Musk's companies, Tesla and SpaceX, tumbled after the billionaires spent hundreds
of millions of dollars trying to elect more Republicans.
Rafael Nam, NPR News.
Around the globe, adolescents are not getting nearly enough exercise according to the World
Health Organization.
More from NPR's Maria Godoy.
Kids and teens should get at least 60 minutes each day of moderate to vigorous physical activity,
like playground play, skateboarding, or soccer.
On average, adolescents reported being active for less than three days a week, a situation
that the WHO says hasn't improved in the last 15 years.
And in almost every country, the report found girls were less likely to be active than boys.
The findings were based on population-based surveys in 140 countries and territories.
They appear in the journal The Lancet Global Health.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Florida Republicans fend off Democratic rivals, including for governor, in midterm elections
Trump says he'd probably get along with Democrats in Congress but retains veto power
Trump says he would go to war with Iran again over its nuclear threat
Democrats win midterm races across lean-Democratic and toss-up House seats despite GOP redistricting
Schumer calls Democratic midterm victories a generational remake of the Senate map
Democrat Annie Andrews flips South Carolina Senate seat, becoming the Senate's first practicing physician since the 1930s
314 Action backed physician candidates, including Abdul El Sayed and Amy Acton, many of whom won
Dow closes up more than 1,500 points as markets react to peaceful election outcome and divided government
World Health Organization report finds adolescents worldwide are not getting enough physical exercise
Girls less likely than boys to be physically active in almost every country, according to WHO survey
